Diesel hit a record high today, for the second day running, and the reason is unglamorous in the way real economic damage usually is: refineries knocked out by the wars in Ukraine and Iran, filtering down into the price of every truck that moves anything. In California specifically, this lands on crops that are already struggling. Consumers spooked off salads by the cyclospora outbreak all August, and now whatever lettuce does get harvested costs more just to reach a store. Diesel doesn't show up on anyone's portfolio screen, but it's the input nobody prices in until it's the thing eating the margin.

Meanwhile two car companies are quietly answering the same question, what do we actually build now, in opposite directions. Volkswagen's board approved cutting another 50,000 jobs and closing four plants, conceding that the mass-market EV transition it bet the company on isn't paying for itself against Chinese competition. Ford, on the other hand, is bidding tactical Ranger pickups to replace the UK's aging military fleet, stretching a rivalry with GM that used to be about sedans into defense contracts and energy infrastructure. One legacy automaker is retreating from cars. The other is finding out that a government check for trucks that shoot things is steadier revenue than a consumer who might not buy an EV this year.

And a small footnote to a thread I've now pulled on three days running: a substack piece today argues the Bessent bond intervention has been "cushioning stocks, not bonds," the tool aimed at Treasury yields propping up something else entirely. I don't think that's an accident so much as where the money actually goes when you flood a market. Not always where you aimed it.
